title: Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose the Disorder, Then Treat the Risk
bottomLine: Suspected OSA requires a sleep-focused history and an appropriate diagnostic sleep study; snoring alone is not the diagnosis. Treat clinically important OSA with PAP or another evidence-based option matched to severity, anatomy, preference and comorbidity, and address driving safety when sleepiness creates risk.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal choking, nonrestorative sleep, morning headache and excessive daytime sleepiness support suspicion.
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, obesity and resistant cardiometabolic disease increase pretest probability but do not replace diagnostic testing.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, circadian disorder, sedating medications, depression and central sleep apnea can mimic or coexist with OSA.
A normal home study does not exclude OSA when pretest probability remains high or the patient is unsuitable for home testing.
assessment: Assess sleep schedule, witnessed breathing events, daytime impairment, driving/work risk, alcohol/sedatives, nasal obstruction, cardiopulmonary disease and prior sleep testing.
Use a validated screening tool only to estimate risk—not to make the diagnosis.
workup: Use home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to patient complexity and local sleep-medicine criteria.
Escalate to in-lab/specialty evaluation when central events, hypoventilation, significant cardiopulmonary disease or an inconclusive home study is possible.
management: Use PAP as a core treatment for clinically significant OSA and optimize mask/interface, humidification, adherence and troubleshooting.
Weight management, positional measures, oral appliance or surgical assessment may be appropriate for selected patients.
Do not manage dangerous daytime sleepiness as routine fatigue; address driving/work restrictions using current Canadian/provincial guidance.
medicationSafety: Alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines and other sedatives can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and daytime impairment.
Do not prescribe chronic sedatives for insomnia before considering OSA when the presentation is suggestive.
redFlags: Dangerous daytime sleepiness while driving/operating equipment
counselling: Explain that PAP efficacy depends on actual nightly use and fit; troubleshoot barriers rather than calling the therapy a failure immediately.
Review sleep duration, alcohol/sedative exposure and driving risk.
followUp: Review objective PAP adherence/effectiveness when available, residual sleepiness, mask problems and cardiometabolic risk.
Reassess the diagnosis if adequate PAP use does not improve symptoms.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from a high screening score without a sleep study—or prescribing a sedative for fatigue/insomnia before asking about apneas and sleepiness.
oneLinePearl: Screening predicts OSA risk; a sleep study establishes the disorder.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disordered-breathing resources
Provincial adult OSA diagnostic and driving-safety pathways

title: Pleural Effusion: Transudate, Exudate, Infection, Malignancy, or Something Else?
bottomLine: A pleural effusion is a syndrome. Decide whether the cause is already clinically obvious and responding, or whether new unilateral/asymmetric, febrile, recurrent or otherwise unexplained fluid requires diagnostic thoracentesis and a malignancy/infection/PE differential.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds/dullness may occur, but small effusions can be incidental.
Bilateral effusions in clear decompensated heart failure may respond to therapy without immediate sampling; atypical or nonresolving features change that decision.
differentiate: Transudative physiology is commonly related to hydrostatic/oncotic forces; exudative fluid raises infection, malignancy, inflammatory disease and other local pleural processes.
Parapneumonic effusion/empyema may need definitive drainage; repeated thoracentesis alone is not adequate source control.
assessment: Assess fever, pleuritic pain, malignancy risk, weight loss, heart/renal/liver disease, VTE risk, recent pneumonia and medication history.
Use ultrasound to confirm size/location before procedure planning.
workup: When sampled, interpret pleural protein/LDH with paired serum values and order pH/glucose, cell count, microbiology or cytology according to the differential.
Use CT or other imaging when malignancy, PE, loculation or another structural cause remains likely.
management: Treat the underlying cause; drain complicated infected pleural collections and coordinate specialty care for malignant/recurrent effusions.
Therapeutic drainage for dyspnea should be monitored for procedure complications and symptom response.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet management around procedures is individualized to urgency, bleeding risk and local guidance.
Do not repeatedly expose a patient to antibiotics for a sterile/recurrent effusion without establishing the cause.
counselling: Explain whether sampling is needed to find the cause or whether treatment of an already-established systemic cause is the safer first step.
followUp: Close the loop on cytology/microbiology and ensure nonresolving effusions receive specialty evaluation.
examTrap: Sampling every bilateral heart-failure effusion immediately—or repeatedly treating an unexplained unilateral effusion without diagnostic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid needs a question: why is it there, and will sampling change the plan?

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize First, Then Find the Airway Bleeding Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis ranges from blood-streaked sputum to life-threatening airway bleeding. First confirm the blood is pulmonary, assess airway/oxygenation/hemodynamics and bleeding burden, then evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE, anticoagulation and other causes.
recognize: True hemoptysis is coughed from the lower respiratory tract; epistaxis/oropharyngeal bleeding and hematemesis can mimic it.
Risk depends more on airway compromise, ongoing bleeding and physiologic effect than on a memorized volume threshold.
differentiate: Infection and bronchiectasis are common causes, but cancer and pulmonary embolism must be considered when risk/context fit.
Anticoagulation can worsen bleeding but should not automatically be assumed to be the primary cause.
assessment: Assess ABCs, oxygenation, hemodynamics, ongoing bleeding, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, smoking history, TB risk, infection symptoms and VTE/cancer clues.
Localize side when possible and look for upper-airway/GI sources.
workup: Use chest radiography initially in many stable patients and CT/CTA when malignancy, vascular source or significant bleeding is suspected.
CBC/coagulation/renal function and type/screen are guided by severity and medication history; sputum/TB testing is context specific.
management: Significant active hemoptysis requires emergency/hospital care, airway planning and respirology/interventional radiology/thoracic support.
Address reversible coagulopathy when clinically appropriate while treating the underlying cause.
Bronchial-artery embolization or other definitive therapy may be required for ongoing significant bleeding.
medicationSafety: Do not reverse anticoagulation reflexively in trivial bleeding without balancing thrombosis risk; major bleeding requires urgent guideline-directed reversal.
Avoid delaying airway control while waiting for complete imaging/lab clarification in unstable bleeding.
counselling: Any recurrent hemoptysis needs follow-up even if the first episode stops, especially with smoking/cancer/TB risk.
followUp: Ensure imaging and specialist follow-up are completed for unexplained/recurrent cases.
examTrap: Calling hemoptysis a benign bronchitis symptom without assessing airway risk or cancer/TB/PE context.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, airway threat matters more than the exact millilitres of blood.
sourceBasis: Canadian TB and anticoagulation guidance where applicable

title: Chronic Cough: Treat the Pattern, Not the Symptom Forever
bottomLine: Chronic cough requires a structured cause search rather than indefinite antitussives or repeated antibiotics. Start with smoking/ACE inhibitor exposure, chest radiograph when indicated, asthma/eosinophilic disease, upper-airway symptoms and reflux clues, while escalating red flags for cancer, TB or ILD.
recognize: Common causes include asthma/eosinophilic airway disease, upper-airway cough syndrome/rhinosinusitis, reflux, smoking and ACE inhibitors.
Multiple causes can coexist, so partial response to one treatment does not always end the evaluation.
differentiate: Persistent cough after infection is different from new hemoptysis, weight loss, focal chest findings or progressive dyspnea.
Cough with normal imaging/spirometry can still reflect asthma/eosinophilic disease, reflux or laryngeal hypersensitivity.
assessment: Ask duration, smoking/vaping, ACE inhibitor use, occupational exposure, nasal symptoms, wheeze, reflux, sputum, hemoptysis, weight loss and TB risk.
Review medication and chest examination; identify whether cough is productive or dry and whether symptoms vary by workplace/environment.
workup: Use chest radiography and spirometry according to the presentation; add bronchoprovocation, eosinophilic testing, CT or specialty evaluation only when the differential warrants it.
Avoid broad repeated antibiotics or repeated normal imaging without a diagnostic question.
management: Stop an ACE inhibitor trial when clinically appropriate, treat documented/suspected asthma/rhinosinusitis/reflux using evidence-based pathways and reassess response.
Refer refractory unexplained cough or red-flag presentations to respirology/ENT as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Opioid antitussives and sedating cough products can cause harm and do not replace diagnosis.
Do not use repeated antibiotics for chronic cough without evidence of bacterial infection.
counselling: Explain that cough treatment often requires sequential trials tied to likely causes rather than one universal cough suppressant.
followUp: Reassess after each targeted intervention and stop ineffective therapies rather than stacking them indefinitely.
examTrap: Giving a third antibiotic for months of cough without checking ACE inhibitor use, spirometry or chest imaging/red flags.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is an algorithm, not an antibiotic diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society cough guidance/endorsed cough algorithms

title: Tuberculosis: Separate Infection From Disease Before You Treat
bottomLine: TST/IGRA identify TB infection risk, not active TB disease. Before preventive therapy, exclude active disease using symptoms, imaging and microbiology when indicated; suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires airborne precautions and public-health coordination immediately.
recognize: Active pulmonary TB may present with chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss or hemoptysis but can be subtle.
TB infection may be asymptomatic and detected through exposure/risk-based testing.
differentiate: A positive TST/IGRA does not distinguish latent/inactive infection from active disease.
BCG history affects TST interpretation more than IGRA and should not be used to dismiss a positive infection test automatically.
assessment: Assess country/region of birth/travel, household/contact exposure, congregate settings, Indigenous/community epidemiology, immunosuppression/HIV, symptoms and prior testing/treatment.
Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing language and ask about barriers to prolonged treatment/follow-up.
workup: For suspected pulmonary disease, use chest imaging and appropriate sputum molecular/microscopy/culture testing through TB/public-health pathways.
For infection testing, choose TST/IGRA according to the Canadian TB Standards and the clinical context; avoid indiscriminate low-risk screening.
management: Active TB disease requires multidrug treatment and public-health/specialist coordination; do not start preventive therapy until active disease is excluded.
Use current Canadian preventive-treatment regimens for eligible infection and monitor adherence/toxicity according to regimen/patient risk.
Initiate airborne precautions promptly for suspected contagious pulmonary/laryngeal TB.
medicationSafety: TB drugs have major hepatic, neurologic, visual and drug-interaction considerations; exact regimen/monitoring follows the Canadian TB Standards and specialty/public-health program.
Rifamycins can substantially alter many medications including hormonal contraception and anticoagulants.
redFlags: Immunocompromised patient with possible active disease
Suspected infectious pulmonary TB in a congregate/health-care setting
counselling: Explain the difference between TB infection and TB disease and why preventive therapy can reduce later disease risk.
Discuss public-health contact processes and adherence support without blame.
followUp: Ensure microbiology, susceptibility, public-health actions and treatment monitoring are closed-loop.
Monitor for post-TB lung disease and recurrence when clinically indicated.
examTrap: Starting latent-TB treatment after a positive IGRA without first excluding active pulmonary disease in a symptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: TB infection tests answer exposure/immunity; active disease needs imaging and microbiology.

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Antibiotics Need Objective Bacterial Evidence
bottomLine: Most acute bronchitis is viral and does not benefit from antibiotics. Suspect pneumonia when symptoms are accompanied by abnormal vital signs, focal respiratory findings, hypoxemia or other objective evidence, and confirm with chest radiography when accessible and clinically appropriate.
recognize: Cough after a viral URI can persist for weeks and sputum colour does not prove bacterial infection.
Pneumonia concern rises with fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal findings, systemic illness and high-risk host factors.
differentiate: Crackles alone do not establish pneumonia in most ambulatory patients.
COPD/asthma exacerbation, PE and heart failure can mimic lower-respiratory infection and require different treatment.
assessment: Check vital signs, oxygen saturation, work of breathing and focal chest findings; assess age/frailty, immune status and cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
Ask duration, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, exposure and aspiration risk.
workup: When pneumonia is clinically plausible and imaging is available, use chest radiography to look for new consolidation rather than prescribing antibiotics from symptoms alone.
Avoid routine chest x-ray in a stable patient with normal vitals and normal respiratory examination when pneumonia probability is low.
management: Treat uncomplicated acute bronchitis with supportive care and return precautions, not antibiotics.
Use current Canadian/local pneumonia guidance for confirmed/strongly suspected bacterial pneumonia and risk-stratify disposition.
Escalate hypoxemia, sepsis, severe frailty or inability to maintain oral intake.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile and resistance.
Avoid opioid cough suppressants and sedating combinations in high-risk older adults unless a clear indication exists.
counselling: Explain expected cough duration and why antibiotics do not treat viral bronchitis.
Give explicit return precautions for worsening dyspnea, fever, chest pain, confusion or dehydration.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms worsen or fail to follow the expected course; do not extend antibiotics automatically for persistent cough alone.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for green sputum and crackles with normal vitals instead of evaluating whether pneumonia is actually present.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis is usually viral; pneumonia needs objective evidence and severity assessment.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely
Choosing Wisely Canada Emergency Medicine recommendations

title: Respiratory Infection in the Immunocompromised Host: Broaden the Differential, Lower the Escalation Threshold
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients can deteriorate rapidly with muted fever or leukocytosis. Define the immune defect and exposure/treatment history, broaden bacterial/viral/fungal/opportunistic possibilities, obtain early imaging/microbiology, and escalate sooner than you would for an otherwise healthy host.
recognize: Neutropenia, transplant, hematologic malignancy, advanced HIV, high-dose steroids/biologics and other immunosuppression produce different pathogen risks.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea or new infiltrates may be more informative than fever in a profoundly immunocompromised patient.
differentiate: Pulmonary edema, drug toxicity, hemorrhage, malignancy and inflammatory pneumonitis can mimic infection.
Pneumocystis, invasive fungal, CMV and other opportunistic infections depend on the specific immune defect and prophylaxis history.
assessment: Define diagnosis/transplant status, neutrophil count, medications/biologics/steroids, prophylaxis, HIV status when relevant, recent hospitalization/antibiotics and travel/exposure.
Assess oxygenation and work of breathing early; do not rely on a benign-appearing temperature alone.
workup: Use early chest imaging and pathogen testing tailored to immune defect; obtain cultures before antibiotics when feasible without delaying treatment in an unstable patient.
Specialty-guided bronchoscopy/BAL or advanced testing may be needed when routine testing is unrevealing.
management: Hospitalize/escalate when oxygenation, hemodynamics, neutropenia or overall immune risk make outpatient care unsafe.
Start empiric antimicrobial therapy promptly when severe infection is plausible and tailor to immune defect, prior organisms and local guidance.
Coordinate infectious disease/oncology/transplant/respirology early.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and drug interactions are critical with azoles, antivirals, transplant drugs and nephrotoxic antibiotics.
Do not stop essential immunosuppression abruptly without specialist input unless an immediate life-threatening reaction demands it.
redFlags: Recent transplant or profound T-cell immunosuppression
counselling: Provide a low threshold for urgent reassessment and ensure the patient knows whom to contact after-hours through the specialty program.
followUp: Track pending cultures/PCR and ensure antimicrobial de-escalation or specialty follow-up occurs when results return.
examTrap: Reassuring a neutropenic patient because there is no high fever despite new hypoxemia and infiltrates.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, the host defect is part of the microbiology differential.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2026 infection-screening guidance where immunosuppression is planned

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Rhinosinusitis: Treat Inflammation, Reserve Antibiotics for the Right Pattern
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory upper-airway disorder; most acute sinus symptoms are viral. Use intranasal anti-inflammatory therapy and allergen measures for rhinitis, and reserve antibiotics for a bacterial rhinosinusitis pattern supported by severity/persistence or failure of an appropriate observation/intranasal-steroid strategy.
recognize: Sneezing, itching, watery rhinorrhea and congestion with seasonal/perennial triggers support allergic rhinitis.
Facial pressure, obstruction, purulent/discoloured drainage and smell reduction can occur in rhinosinusitis but do not automatically prove bacterial infection.
differentiate: Viral URI is far more common than acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.
Unilateral severe pain/swelling, orbital symptoms, neurologic symptoms, dental source or recurrent unilateral disease requires a different workup.
assessment: Assess duration/pattern, allergen exposure, asthma, medication use, pregnancy, prior sinus surgery, dental symptoms and red flags.
Review decongestant overuse and intranasal spray technique.
workup: Routine sinus imaging is not required for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis; use imaging for complications, atypical/recurrent disease or specialty planning.
Allergy testing is useful when results will change avoidance/immunotherapy decisions, not as a universal panel.
management: Use intranasal corticosteroid, saline and appropriate antihistamine strategies for allergic rhinitis.
For uncomplicated suspected bacterial sinusitis, follow current Canadian stewardship criteria; many mild/moderate cases can begin with intranasal corticosteroids/observation before antibiotics.
Refer recurrent/chronic or anatomically complicated disease to ENT/allergy when indicated.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestants can cause rebound congestion with prolonged use; oral decongestants can worsen hypertension/arrhythmia and insomnia.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for viral disease and choose pregnancy-compatible therapy when relevant.
redFlags: Immunocompromised patient with severe sinus disease
counselling: Teach intranasal spray direction/technique and expected time to benefit.
Explain why coloured mucus alone does not prove bacterial infection.
followUp: Reassess failure to improve, recurrence or persistent symptoms rather than repeatedly prescribing empiric antibiotics.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for three days of congestion and green discharge without a bacterial pattern or complications.
oneLinePearl: Most sinus symptoms are inflammatory/viral; antibiotics need the right time-course and severity pattern.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely primary-care resources
